questions.q: What is a "zone of trust" in the context of IAM Access Analyzer?
options: The account or AWS Organization the analyzer treats as trusted — access reaching in from outside it is what generates a finding
A list of IP ranges allowed to call the AWS API
A VPC configuration that isolates resources from the public internet
A setting that determines how long temporary credentials remain valid
questions.explain: You choose a zone of trust — a single account or an entire Organization — when creating an analyzer. Anything inside it is trusted by default; a principal outside it reaching a resource inside it produces an external access finding.

questions.q: In the example external access finding for the "ltv-shared-reports" S3 bucket, what three pieces of information does the finding give you?
options: Only the bucket's creation date and storage class
Only the number of objects in the bucket
Which external principal can reach the resource, what actions it can perform, and whether any condition narrows that access
Only whether the bucket has versioning enabled
questions.explain: A finding reports the external principal, the specific actions it's permitted (e.g. s3:GetObject, s3:ListBucket), and any condition — everything needed to decide whether the access is intentional or a mistake.

questions.q: What does an unused access finding for "unused permissions" flag, as distinct from an unused IAM role finding?
options: That the entire role has never been assumed by anyone
That the account has no IAM roles defined at all
That the role's trust policy is misconfigured
That individual actions granted by a policy have never actually been called by the principal, even though the role itself is active and in use
questions.explain: Unused permissions findings target the gap between permissions as written and permissions as actually used — a role can be active daily and still have unused actions sitting in its policy that a leaked credential could still exploit.

questions.q: What does the check-no-new-access custom policy check do?
options: It deletes any IAM role that hasn't been used in 90 days
It automatically archives every external access finding without review
It compares a proposed policy change against a reference policy and reports whether the change grants access beyond what was already allowed, before deployment
It blocks all S3 bucket policies from ever including a Condition
questions.explain: check-no-new-access is a custom policy check meant to run before a policy change is deployed — often in CI/CD — comparing the proposed policy to a reference and flagging any newly granted access.

questions.q: Why would a security team set up an archive rule for an external access finding on a vendor's S3 access, rather than just deleting the finding?
options: Because deleting findings is technically impossible in Access Analyzer
Because archive rules automatically revoke the vendor's access once applied
Because an archive rule only works on unused access findings, never external access findings
Because the access is genuinely intentional, and an archive rule auto-archives future findings matching that known pattern so it doesn't resurface as noise on every re-scan
questions.explain: Archive rules are for findings that represent intentional, reviewed access — like a vendor's legitimate read access to a reporting bucket — so the same known-good grant doesn't have to be re-reviewed every time the analyzer scans again.
